# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

starting the server.

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

# SMA-820: Gemini translator merges same-role contents and names each tool result from its own call

Linear: [SMA-820](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-820/gemini-translator-sends-two-adjacent-user-contents-after-a-tool-result).
Size: a small change, in one file (`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini/src/translate/request.rs`) and its snapshots.

## Intent

`items_to_contents` makes one Gemini content for each core `Item`. Two defects follow:

1. **Adjacent same-role contents.** A tool result becomes a `role: user` content with a
   `functionResponse` part. When a user message comes directly after it, the request has two
   adjacent `role: user` contents. Two paths cause this: a turn-boundary checkpoint that returns
   `Inject(..)` after a tool turn (PR #346), and a resumed run after a deferred tool call.
2. **Wrong name on a repeated call id.** The translator resolves a `functionResponse` name from one
   global `call_id -> name` map, and the last call wins. `stream.rs` makes the fallback ids
   `fc_{n}` per stream, so two turns can both have a call `fc_0`. Then an earlier result gets the
   name of a later call (turn 1 `search`/`fc_0`, turn 2 `pay`/`fc_0` → the `search` result is sent
   as `pay`).

## Goals

- The translator never sends two adjacent contents with the same role. It merges them into one
  content and keeps the order of the parts.
- The rule applies to every item, so replayed session items are also covered.
- Each `functionResponse` gets the name of its own call.

## Non-goals

- Gemini thought signatures and `ContentPart::Reasoning` translation (still deferred, D3).
- Changes to the fallback id scheme in `stream.rs`.
- Changes to other providers.

## Approaches

1. **Merge after translation (picked).** Translate each item to `(role, parts)` as today, then fold
   adjacent entries with the same role into one content. One small post-pass. It covers every
   source of adjacency (tool results, parallel calls, assistant text + call, replay) with one rule.
2. **Merge at each push site.** Each branch checks the last content and appends to it. This repeats
   the same check in five branches, and a new branch can forget it.
3. **Reorder items in core before the provider sees them.** Rejected: the problem is a Gemini wire
   rule, and other providers accept the core order as it is.

Sven approved approach 1 on 2026-11-20.

## Design

### Merge

- Build a `Vec<(role, Vec<Value>)>` in item order, then fold it: when the role of an entry equals
  the role of the last merged entry, append its parts; else start a new content.
- An entry with no parts is dropped before the fold (my call, approved). Today only an empty
  `user` content is dropped; an assistant message with only `Reasoning` parts gives a `model`
  content with `"parts": []`.
- `Item::System` stays in `systemInstruction` and does not take part in the merge.
- Items that the translator skips (`_ => {}`) do not break adjacency: the contents on either side
  of a skipped item merge if they have the same role.
- Consequences that are intended:
  - Parallel calls: N adjacent `ToolCall` items become one `model` content with N `functionCall`
    parts, and N results become one `user` content with N `functionResponse` parts.
  - An assistant text followed by its `ToolCall` becomes one `model` content (text part, then
    `functionCall` part). This is the shape that Gemini itself streams.
- The empty-conversation error stays: if no content remains after the fold, return the error.

### Name resolution

- Replace the global map with one pass in item order, before or during translation, that keeps a
  stack of open call names for each call id.
  - A `ToolCall` item, or a `ContentPart::ToolUse` in an `AssistantMessage`, pushes its name onto
    the stack for its id, and also records it as the most recent call for that id.
  - A result (`Item::ToolResult`, or `ContentPart::ToolResult` in a `UserMessage`) pops the top of
    the stack for its id: the most recent earlier call with that id that has no result yet.
  - If the stack is empty, the result takes the name of the most recent earlier call with that id
    (my call, approved). This keeps a duplicate result for one call working.
  - If no earlier call with that id exists, return the existing
    `tool result references unknown call_id` error.
- Behavior change (my call, approved): a result that comes before its call now gives an error.
  Today the global map accepts it.

## Tests

- Change `tool_result_then_user_message_request_shape` to assert one merged `role: user` content
  with the `functionResponse` part, then the text part.
- New: more than two adjacent contents with the same role merge into one, in order (for example a
  result, then two user messages).
- New: two calls that share `fc_0` with different names (`search`, then `pay` in a later turn);
  assert `search` on the first `functionResponse` and `pay` on the second.
- New: an empty-parts `model` content (reasoning-only assistant message) is dropped and does not
  split its neighbours.
- New: a result before its call gives an error.
- Update the snapshots `snap_parallel_same_name_tool_calls` and any other snapshot that the merge

# SMA-820: Gemini translator merges same-role contents and names each tool result from its own call

Linear: [SMA-820](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-820/gemini-translator-sends-two-adjacent-user-contents-after-a-tool-result).
Size: a small change, in one file (`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini/src/translate/request.rs`) and its snapshots.

## Intent

`items_to_contents` makes one Gemini content for each core `Item`. Two defects follow:

1. **Adjacent same-role contents.** A tool result becomes a `role: user` content with a
   `functionResponse` part. When a user message comes directly after it, the request has two
   adjacent `role: user` contents. Two paths cause this: a turn-boundary checkpoint that returns
   `Inject(..)` after a tool turn (PR #346), and a resumed run after a deferred tool call.
2. **Wrong name on a repeated call id.** The translator resolves a `functionResponse` name from one
   global `call_id -> name` map, and the last call wins. `stream.rs` makes the fallback ids
   `fc_{n}` per stream, so two turns can both have a call `fc_0`. Then an earlier result gets the
   name of a later call (turn 1 `search`/`fc_0`, turn 2 `pay`/`fc_0` → the `search` result is sent
   as `pay`).

## Goals

- The translator never sends two adjacent contents with the same role. It merges them into one
  content and keeps the order of the parts.
- The rule applies to every item, so replayed session items are also covered.
- Each `functionResponse` gets the name of its own call.

## Non-goals

- Gemini thought signatures and `ContentPart::Reasoning` translation (still deferred, D3).
- Changes to the fallback id scheme in `stream.rs`.
- Changes to other providers.

## Approaches

1. **Merge after translation (picked).** Translate each item to `(role, parts)` as today, then fold
   adjacent entries with the same role into one content. One small post-pass. It covers every
   source of adjacency (tool results, parallel calls, assistant text + call, replay) with one rule.
2. **Merge at each push site.** Each branch checks the last content and appends to it. This repeats
   the same check in five branches, and a new branch can forget it.
3. **Reorder items in core before the provider sees them.** Rejected: the problem is a Gemini wire
   rule, and other providers accept the core order as it is.

Sven approved approach 1 on 2026-11-20.

## Design

### Merge

- Build a `Vec<(role, Vec<Value>)>` in item order, then fold it: when the role of an entry equals
  the role of the last merged entry, append its parts; else start a new content.
- An entry with no parts is dropped before the fold (my call, approved). Today only an empty
  `user` content is dropped; an assistant message with only `Reasoning` parts gives a `model`
  content with `"parts": []`.
- `Item::System` stays in `systemInstruction` and does not take part in the merge.
- Items that the translator skips (`_ => {}`) do not break adjacency: the contents on either side
  of a skipped item merge if they have the same role.
- Consequences that are intended:
  - Parallel calls: N adjacent `ToolCall` items become one `model` content with N `functionCall`
    parts, and N results become one `user` content with N `functionResponse` parts.
  - An assistant text followed by its `ToolCall` becomes one `model` content (text part, then
    `functionCall` part). This is the shape that Gemini itself streams.
- The empty-conversation error stays: if no content remains after the fold, return the error.

### Name resolution

- Replace the global map with one pass in item order, before or during translation, that keeps a
  stack of open call names for each call id.
  - A `ToolCall` item, or a `ContentPart::ToolUse` in an `AssistantMessage`, pushes its name onto
    the stack for its id, and also records it as the most recent call for that id.
  - A result (`Item::ToolResult`, or `ContentPart::ToolResult` in a `UserMessage`) pops the top of
    the stack for its id: the most recent earlier call with that id that has no result yet.
  - If the stack is empty, the result takes the name of the most recent earlier call with that id
    (my call, approved). This keeps a duplicate result for one call working.
  - If no earlier call with that id exists, return the existing
    `tool result references unknown call_id` error.
- Behavior change (my call, approved): a result that comes before its call now gives an error.
  Today the global map accepts it.

## Tests

- Change `tool_result_then_user_message_request_shape` to assert one merged `role: user` content
  with the `functionResponse` part, then the text part.
- New: more than two adjacent contents with the same role merge into one, in order (for example a
  result, then two user messages).
- New: two calls that share `fc_0` with different names (`search`, then `pay` in a later turn);
  assert `search` on the first `functionResponse` and `pay` on the second.
- New: an empty-parts `model` content (reasoning-only assistant message) is dropped and does not
  split its neighbours.
- New: a result before its call gives an error.
- Update the snapshots `snap_parallel_same_name_tool_calls` and any other snapshot that the merge
  changes; review each snapshot diff by hand.

## Live check (acceptance criterion)

The probe `probe.sh` (kept in the session scratchpad, not committed) sends hand-made request bodies
to `gemini-2.5-flash` through the REST API, and prints the HTTP status and the finish reason for
each shape. The results go here before and after the fix.

- Before: _pending: Sven runs the probe; the agent cannot read `.env`._
- After: _pending._

## Left to the builder

- The exact helper names and whether the name pass runs as a separate pre-pass or inside the main
  loop.
- Whether to add an "after" live test to `tests/live.rs` (ignored by default) or keep the probe only.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# SMA-820 live probe: how does the Gemini API handle each contents shape?
# Needs GEMINI_API_KEY in the environment. Never prints the key.
set -u
MODEL="${1:-gemini-2.5-flash}"
URL="https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/${MODEL}:generateContent"
TOOLS='[{"functionDeclarations":[
  {"name":"search","description":"Search the web","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"q":{"type":"string"}}}},
  {"name":"pay","description":"Pay a bill","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"amount":{"type":"number"}}}}]}]'

U()   { printf '{"role":"user","parts":[{"text":"%s"}]}' "$1"; }
FC()  { printf '{"functionCall":{"id":"%s","name":"%s","args":%s}}' "$1" "$2" "$3"; }
FR()  { printf '{"functionResponse":{"id":"%s","name":"%s","response":%s}}' "$1" "$2" "$3"; }
M()   { printf '{"role":"model","parts":[%s]}' "$1"; }
UP()  { printf '{"role":"user","parts":[%s]}' "$1"; }

run() {
  local label="$1" contents="$2"
  local body; body=$(printf '{"contents":[%s],"tools":%s}' "$contents" "$TOOLS")
  local out; out=$(curl -sS -w '\n%{http_code}' -H "x-goog-api-key: ${GEMINI_API_KEY}" \
      -H 'content-type: application/json' -d "$body" "$URL")
  local code; code=$(tail -n1 <<<"$out")
  local json; json=$(sed '$d' <<<"$out")
  local summary
  summary=$(jq -c '{err: .error.message, finish: .candidates[0].finishReason,
     parts: [.candidates[0].content.parts[]? | (.text // ("functionCall:" + .functionCall.name))[0:80]]}' <<<"$json" 2>/dev/null)
  printf '%-34s HTTP %s %s\n' "$label" "$code" "$summary"
}

S1='{"q":"cats"}'; R1='{"hits":3}'
echo "model=$MODEL"
run "1 baseline call+result" \
  "$(U 'search cats'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 search "$S1")"),$(UP "$(FR fc_0 search "$R1")")"
run "2 result + adjacent user text" \
  "$(U 'search cats'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 search "$S1")"),$(UP "$(FR fc_0 search "$R1")"),$(U 'Also: answer in French.')"
run "3 result + text merged" \
  "$(U 'search cats'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 search "$S1")"),$(UP "$(FR fc_0 search "$R1"),{\"text\":\"Also: answer in French.\"}")"
run "4 three adjacent user contents" \
  "$(U 'search cats'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 search "$S1")"),$(UP "$(FR fc_0 search "$R1")"),$(U 'Also:'),$(U 'answer in French.')"
run "5 parallel split (2 model,2 user)" \
  "$(U 'search a and b'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 search '{"q":"a"}')"),$(M "$(FC fc_1 search '{"q":"b"}')"),$(UP "$(FR fc_0 search '{"n":1}')"),$(UP "$(FR fc_1 search '{"n":2}')")"
run "6 parallel merged" \
  "$(U 'search a and b'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 search '{"q":"a"}'),$(FC fc_1 search '{"q":"b"}')"),$(UP "$(FR fc_0 search '{"n":1}'),$(FR fc_1 search '{"n":2}')")"
run "7 response name != call name" \
  "$(U 'search cats'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 search "$S1")"),$(UP "$(FR fc_0 pay "$R1")")"
REPEAT_HEAD="$(U 'search cats'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 search "$S1")")"
REPEAT_MID="$(M '{"text":"3 hits."}'),$(U 'now pay 5'),$(M "$(FC fc_0 pay '{"amount":5}')"),$(UP "$(FR fc_0 pay '{"ok":true}')")"

# SMA-820: Gemini translator merges same-role contents and names each tool result from its own call

Linear: [SMA-820](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-820/gemini-translator-sends-two-adjacent-user-contents-after-a-tool-result).
Size: a small change in the Gemini translator. Files: `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini/src/translate/request.rs`,
`.../src/translate/mod.rs` (inline asserts in `snap_parallel_same_name_tool_calls`), the snapshots in
`.../src/translate/snapshots/`, and `.../tests/live.rs`.

## Intent

`items_to_contents` makes one Gemini content for each core `Item`. Two defects follow.

1. **Adjacent same-role contents.** A tool result becomes a `role: user` content with a
   `functionResponse` part. When a user message comes directly after it, the request has two
   adjacent `role: user` contents. Known sources of this shape:
   - a turn-boundary checkpoint that returns `Inject(..)` after a tool turn (PR #346);
   - a resumed run after a deferred tool call;
   - a synthetic cancel result followed by the input of the next run;
   - the handoff transcript note after a user message, when the transfer turn had no text
     (`crates/paigasus-helikon-core/src/loop_state.rs:770-789`);
   - the `CompactingSession` prompt after a snapshot that ends in a tool result.
   Parallel calls also give adjacent `model` contents (one per `ToolCall`) and adjacent `user`
   contents (one per result).
2. **Wrong name on a repeated call id.** The translator resolves a `functionResponse` name from one
   global `call_id -> name` map, and the last call wins. `stream.rs` makes the fallback ids
   `fc_{n}` per stream, so two turns can both have a call `fc_0`. Then an earlier result gets the
   name of a later call (turn 1 `search`/`fc_0`, turn 2 `pay`/`fc_0` → the `search` result is sent
   as `pay`).

## Goals

- The translator never sends two adjacent contents with the same role. It merges them into one
  content and keeps the order of the parts.
- The rule applies to every item, so replayed session items are also covered.
- Each `functionResponse` gets the name of the call that it closes, by the core pairing rule
  (below), within the limits in "Known limits".

## Non-goals

- Gemini thought signatures and `ContentPart::Reasoning` translation (still deferred, D3).
- Changes to the fallback id scheme in `stream.rs`. A unique fallback id would remove the collision
  for new histories, but stored sessions already hold repeated `fc_0` ids, so the translator must
  pair by order anyway. A follow-up Linear issue can track the id scheme.
- Changes to other providers.

## Approaches

1. **Merge after translation (picked).** Translate each item to `(role, parts)` as today, then fold
   adjacent entries with the same role into one content. One small post-pass covers every source
   of adjacency with one rule.
2. **Merge at each push site.** Each branch checks the last content and appends to it. This repeats
   the same check in five branches, and a new branch can forget it.
3. **Reorder items in core before the provider sees them.** Rejected: the problem is a Gemini wire
   rule, and other providers accept the core order as it is.

Sven approved approach 1 on 2026-11-20.

## Design

### Merge

- Build a `Vec<(role, Vec<Value>)>` in item order, then fold it: when the role of an entry equals
  the role of the last merged entry, append its parts; else start a new content.
- An entry with no parts is dropped before the fold. Today only an empty `user` content is
  dropped. An assistant message with only `Reasoning` parts gives a `model` content with
  `"parts": []`.
- An empty `ContentPart::Text` (`text == ""`) in a user or assistant message is dropped (SMA-804
  spec §5.3 asks every translator to do this; SMA-819 did it for Anthropic). Without this, the
  merge puts `{"text": ""}` into the content with the `functionResponse`.
- `Item::System` stays in `systemInstruction` and does not take part in the merge. Items that the
  translator skips, and `System` items, do not break adjacency.
- Intended consequences:
  - Parallel calls: N adjacent `ToolCall` items become one `model` content with N `functionCall`
    parts, and N results become one `user` content with N `functionResponse` parts.
  - An assistant text followed by its `ToolCall` becomes one `model` content (text part, then
    `functionCall` part).
  - Two adjacent user texts become two `text` parts in one content. They are not joined.
- The order of parallel `functionCall` parts is the core item order. `build_items` in core emits
  calls in `BTreeMap<call_id, _>` order (`crates/paigasus-helikon-core/src/model.rs:514,530`), so
  `fc_10` comes before `fc_2`. This spec does not change that. Note for D3: Gemini 3 puts the
  thought signature on the first `functionCall` part.
- The empty-conversation error stays: if no content remains after the fold, return the error.

### Name resolution (core pairing rule, FIFO)

- One pass in item order. The pass keeps a list of open calls (call id, name), in order. The
  translator must not store names by call id in a pre-pass, because that brings the defect back.
  The open-call state goes `&mut` into `user_parts`, or the pass stores names by occurrence.
  - A `ToolCall` item, or a `ContentPart::ToolUse` in an `AssistantMessage`, adds an open call.
  - A result (`Item::ToolResult`, or `ContentPart::ToolResult` in a `UserMessage`) closes the
    **earliest** open call with its id and takes that name.
- This is the rule that core uses: `resume_exec::paired_result` (`resume_exec.rs:200-220`, "each
  result closes the earliest open call with its call id", "as in the session recorder") and
  `deferral::agent_view` (`deferral.rs:585-620`). `run_tools_concurrent` returns one outcome per
  call in call order (`agent.rs:748`). With FIFO, two calls in one round that share `fc_0` get the
  correct names. The cross-turn `search`/`pay` case also works.
  - **This changes the ticket text.** The ticket says "the most recent earlier call with the same
    id that has no result yet" (LIFO). LIFO gives both names wrong for two same-id calls in one
    round, where `main` gives one of two. Sven decides at GATE 1.
- A result that closes no open call, but that has an earlier call with its id (a second result for
  one call), is **dropped** with a `tracing::warn!` (target `paigasus::gemini::translate`). This
  matches `agent_view`, which drops a result that closes no open call. It also prevents a merged
  `user` content with more `functionResponse` parts than its `functionCall` parts. (This replaces
  the earlier call "use the most recent earlier call", which could send two responses for one
  call.)
- A result whose id has no earlier call returns an error:
  - if a later item has a call with that id: a new message, `tool result for call_id {id} comes
    before its call`;
  - else the existing `tool result references unknown call_id {id}`.
- Behavior change: a result before its call now gives an error. Today the global map accepts it.
  No core producer makes this order: `close_open_transfers` inserts at `at + 1`
  (`resume_exec.rs:194`), the resume block follows the calls of the earlier run, and the legacy
  repair moves results after their calls. A stored session in this order now fails at `invoke`
  instead of being sent. The commit message names this error so that the CHANGELOG shows it.

### Invariant and known limits

The merge depends on one invariant: the next `user` content answers each `functionCall` of a
`model` content. Two real core histories do not hold it:

1. **Open deferred calls.** `RunDeferred` leaves calls with no result. `CompactingSession` sends
   `snapshot + prompt` to its model (`compacting_session.rs:200-211`). With a Gemini summarizer
   this gives, for example, `model[fc c1, fc c2], user[fr c1, text]`. Probe shape 14 shows what
   Gemini does with it. This spec does not add synthetic results; if shape 14 fails, a follow-up
   issue covers it.
2. **Replay of a `ParallelAgent` session.** Sibling events interleave through `select_all`
   (`workflow.rs:377`), and sibling Gemini agents all start at `fc_0`. The merge can put two
   `functionCall` parts with the same id into one content. No order rule can name those results
   correctly. This spec does not fix it.

## Tests

Unit tests in `request.rs` assert the full `contents` array, as
`tool_result_then_user_message_request_shape` does:

- Change `tool_result_then_user_message_request_shape` (and its doc comment) to one merged
  `role: user` content: the `functionResponse` part, then the text part.
- More than two adjacent contents with the same role merge into one, in order (a result, then two
  user messages).
- Two calls in different turns that share `fc_0` (`search`, then `pay`): correct name on each
  `functionResponse`.
- Two calls in one round that share `fc_0` (`search`, then `pay`), as two `ToolCall` items and as
  two `ToolUse` parts in one `AssistantMessage`: the first result is `search`, the second `pay`.
- Results in a different order than the calls (distinct ids): each gets its own name.
- A second result for one call is dropped.
- A result before its call gives the new error.
- A nested `ContentPart::ToolResult` mixed with `Text` in a `UserMessage`, directly after an
  `Item::ToolResult`: one merged `user` content with correct names.
- An `Item::System` between two user messages: one merged `user` content.
- A reasoning-only assistant message is dropped and its neighbours merge.
- An empty `Text` part is dropped.

Snapshots: update `snap_parallel_same_name_tool_calls` and its inline asserts in `mod.rs`, and any
other snapshot that the merge changes. Review each snapshot diff by hand.

Live test (mandatory, `#[ignore]` in `tests/live.rs`, needs `GEMINI_API_KEY`): call
`GeminiModel::invoke` with `search` and `pay` declared, for three histories: the SMA-804 shape
(result then user text), one parallel round, and a cross-turn `fc_0` collision. Assert no `Err`
event and a `Finish` event. This is the "after" check through the real translator.

## Live check (acceptance criterion)

The probe `probe.sh` sends hand-made request bodies to `gemini-2.5-flash` through the REST API
(`generateContent`), with `search` and `pay` declared. It prints the HTTP status, the finish reason
and a short part summary. It never prints request headers. The probe source goes into the commit
body. Shapes:

1. baseline: `user, model[fc], user[fr]`
2. SMA-804 today: `..., user[fr], user[text]`
3. SMA-804 merged: `..., user[fr, text]`
4. three adjacent `user` contents
5. parallel today: `model[fc0], model[fc1], user[fr0], user[fr1]`
6. parallel merged: `model[fc0, fc1], user[fr0, fr1]`
7. `functionResponse` name differs from its `functionCall` name
8. repeated `fc_0` across turns, correct names
9. repeated `fc_0` across turns, today's wrong name
10. `model[text, fc]`
11. parallel merged, responses in a different order than the calls
12. `user[fr, {"text": ""}]`
13. two `functionResponse` parts for one call
14. parallel merged, one call has no response, then text

Pass rule for a target shape (3, 6, 8, 10, 11): HTTP 200, `finishReason: STOP`, and an answer that
uses the tool result.

Order: run the probe **before** any code. If Gemini rejects shape 3 or 6, stop and bring it back to
Sven before implementation (fallback: keep the merge for `model` contents only, or put the text in a
separate content after a synthetic `model` turn; Sven decides).

Results:

- Before (probe, hand-made bodies): _pending, Sven runs the probe; the agent cannot read `.env`._
- After (live test through the translator): _pending._

Scope of the check: Developer API and `gemini-2.5-flash` only. Vertex uses the same translator.
Gemini 3 needs thought signatures for function calls, so hand-made bodies with no signatures can
fail on 3.x for a different reason; Gemini 3 is out of scope here.

## Docs and release

- No book or README page describes the old shape, so no book or README edit is needed.
- release-plz bumps `paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini` (patch) and the facade by cascade. No hand
  version bump.

## Left to the builder

- Helper names, and how the open-call state reaches `user_parts`, within the one-pass rule above.

Linear: [SMA-820](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-820/gemini-translator-sends-two-adjacent-user-contents-after-a-tool-result).
Size: a small change in the Gemini translator. Files: `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini/src/translate/request.rs`,
`.../src/translate/mod.rs` (inline asserts in `snap_parallel_same_name_tool_calls`), the snapshots in
`.../src/translate/snapshots/`, and `.../tests/live.rs`.

## Intent

`items_to_contents` makes one Gemini content for each core `Item`. Two defects follow.

1. **Adjacent same-role contents.** A tool result becomes a `role: user` content with a
   `functionResponse` part. When a user message comes directly after it, the request has two
   adjacent `role: user` contents. Known sources of this shape:
   - a turn-boundary checkpoint that returns `Inject(..)` after a tool turn (PR #346);
   - a resumed run after a deferred tool call;
   - a synthetic cancel result followed by the input of the next run;
   - the handoff transcript note after a user message, when the transfer turn had no text
     (`crates/paigasus-helikon-core/src/loop_state.rs:770-789`);
   - the `CompactingSession` prompt after a snapshot that ends in a tool result.
   Parallel calls also give adjacent `model` contents (one per `ToolCall`) and adjacent `user`
   contents (one per result).
2. **Wrong name on a repeated call id.** The translator resolves a `functionResponse` name from one
   global `call_id -> name` map, and the last call wins. `stream.rs` makes the fallback ids
   `fc_{n}` per stream, so two turns can both have a call `fc_0`. Then an earlier result gets the
   name of a later call (turn 1 `search`/`fc_0`, turn 2 `pay`/`fc_0` → the `search` result is sent
   as `pay`).

## Goals

- The translator never sends two adjacent contents with the same role. It merges them into one
  content and keeps the order of the parts.
- The rule applies to every item, so replayed session items are also covered.
- Each `functionResponse` gets the name of the call that it closes, by the core pairing rule
  (below), within the limits in "Known limits".

## Non-goals

- Gemini thought signatures and `ContentPart::Reasoning` translation (still deferred, D3).
- Changes to the fallback id scheme in `stream.rs`. A unique fallback id would remove the collision
  for new histories, but stored sessions already hold repeated `fc_0` ids, so the translator must
  pair by order anyway. A follow-up Linear issue can track the id scheme.
- Changes to other providers.

## Approaches

1. **Merge after translation (picked).** Translate each item to `(role, parts)` as today, then fold
   adjacent entries with the same role into one content. One small post-pass covers every source
   of adjacency with one rule.
2. **Merge at each push site.** Each branch checks the last content and appends to it. This repeats
   the same check in five branches, and a new branch can forget it.
3. **Reorder items in core before the provider sees them.** Rejected: the problem is a Gemini wire
   rule, and other providers accept the core order as it is.

Sven approved approach 1 on 2026-11-20.

## Design

### Merge

- Build a `Vec<(role, Vec<Value>)>` in item order, then fold it: when the role of an entry equals
  the role of the last merged entry, append its parts; else start a new content.
- An entry with no parts is dropped before the fold. Today only an empty `user` content is
  dropped. An assistant message with only `Reasoning` parts gives a `model` content with
  `"parts": []`.

  spec §5.3 asks every translator to do this; SMA-819 did it for Anthropic). Without this, the
  merge puts `{"text": ""}` into the content with the `functionResponse`.

  translator skips, and `System` items, do not break adjacency.
- Intended consequences:

    parts, and N results become one `user` content with N `functionResponse` parts.
  - An assistant text followed by its `ToolCall` becomes one `model` content (text part, then
    `functionCall` part).
  - Two adjacent user texts become two `text` parts in one content. They are not joined.

  calls in `BTreeMap<call_id, _>` order (`crates/paigasus-helikon-core/src/model.rs:514,530`), so

  thought signature on the first `functionCall` part.

    **earliest** open call with its id and takes that name.

  correct names. The cross-turn `search`/`pay` case also works.

    id that has no result yet" (LIFO). LIFO gives both names wrong for two same-id calls in one

  repair moves results after their calls. A stored session in this order now fails at `invoke`
  instead of being sent. The commit message names this error so that the CHANGELOG shows it.

   correctly. This spec does not fix it.

# SMA-820: Gemini translator merges same-role contents and names each tool result from its own call

Linear: [SMA-820](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-820/gemini-translator-sends-two-adjacent-user-contents-after-a-tool-result).
Size: a small change, in one file (`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-gemini/src/translate/request.rs`) and its snapshots.

## Intent

`items_to_contents` makes one Gemini content for each core `Item`. Two defects follow:

1. **Adjacent same-role contents.** A tool result becomes a `role: user` content with a
   `functionResponse` part. When a user message comes directly after it, the request has two
   adjacent `role: user` contents. Two paths cause this: a turn-boundary checkpoint that returns
   `Inject(..)` after a tool turn (PR #346), and a resumed run after a deferred tool call.
2. **Wrong name on a repeated call id.** The translator resolves a `functionResponse` name from one
   global `call_id -> name` map, and the last call wins. `stream.rs` makes the fallback ids
   `fc_{n}` per stream, so two turns can both have a call `fc_0`. Then an earlier result gets the
   name of a later call (turn 1 `search`/`fc_0`, turn 2 `pay`/`fc_0` → the `search` result is sent
   as `pay`).

## Goals

- The translator never sends two adjacent contents with the same role. It merges them into one
  content and keeps the order of the parts.
- The rule applies to every item, so replayed session items are also covered.
- Each `functionResponse` gets the name of its own call.

## Non-goals

- Gemini thought signatures and `ContentPart::Reasoning` translation (still deferred, D3).
- Changes to the fallback id scheme in `stream.rs`.
- Changes to other providers.

## Approaches

1. **Merge after translation (picked).** Translate each item to `(role, parts)` as today, then fold
   adjacent entries with the same role into one content. One small post-pass. It covers every
   source of adjacency (tool results, parallel calls, assistant text + call, replay) with one rule.
2. **Merge at each push site.** Each branch checks the last content and appends to it. This repeats
   the same check in five branches, and a new branch can forget it.
3. **Reorder items in core before the provider sees them.** Rejected: the problem is a Gemini wire
   rule, and other providers accept the core order as it is.

Sven approved approach 1 on 2026-11-20.

## Design

### Merge

- Build a `Vec<(role, Vec<Value>)>` in item order, then fold it: when the role of an entry equals
  the role of the last merged entry, append its parts; else start a new content.
- An entry with no parts is dropped before the fold (my call, approved). Today only an empty
  `user` content is dropped; an assistant message with only `Reasoning` parts gives a `model`
  content with `"parts": []`.
- `Item::System` stays in `systemInstruction` and does not take part in the merge.
- Items that the translator skips (`_ => {}`) do not break adjacency: the contents on either side
  of a skipped item merge if they have the same role.
- Consequences that are intended:
  - Parallel calls: N adjacent `ToolCall` items become one `model` content with N `functionCall`
    parts, and N results become one `user` content with N `functionResponse` parts.
  - An assistant text followed by its `ToolCall` becomes one `model` content (text part, then
    `functionCall` part). This is the shape that Gemini itself streams.
- The empty-conversation error stays: if no content remains after the fold, return the error.

### Name resolution

- Replace the global map with one pass in item order, before or during translation, that keeps a
  stack of open call names for each call id.
  - A `ToolCall` item, or a `ContentPart::ToolUse` in an `AssistantMessage`, pushes its name onto
    the stack for its id, and also records it as the most recent call for that id.
  - A result (`Item::ToolResult`, or `ContentPart::ToolResult` in a `UserMessage`) pops the top of
    the stack for its id: the most recent earlier call with that id that has no result yet.
  - If the stack is empty, the result takes the name of the most recent earlier call with that id
    (my call, approved). This keeps a duplicate result for one call working.
  - If no earlier call with that id exists, return the existing
    `tool result references unknown call_id` error.
- Behavior change (my call, approved): a result that comes before its call now gives an error.
  Today the global map accepts it.

## Tests

- Change `tool_result_then_user_message_request_shape` to assert one merged `role: user` content
  with the `functionResponse` part, then the text part.
- New: more than two adjacent contents with the same role merge into one, in order (for example a
  result, then two user messages).
- New: two calls that share `fc_0` with different names (`search`, then `pay` in a later turn);
  assert `search` on the first `functionResponse` and `pay` on the second.
- New: an empty-parts `model` content (reasoning-only assistant message) is dropped and does not
  split its neighbours.
- New: a result before its call gives an error.
- Update the snapshots `snap_parallel_same_name_tool_calls` and any other snapshot that the merge
  changes; review each snapshot diff by hand.

## Live check (acceptance criterion)

The probe `probe.sh` (kept in the session scratchpad, not committed) sends hand-made request bodies
to `gemini-2.5-flash` through the REST API, and prints the HTTP status and the finish reason for
each shape. The results go here before and after the fix.

- Before: _pending: Sven runs the probe; the agent cannot read `.env`._
- After: _pending._

## Left to the builder

- The exact helper names and whether the name pass runs as a separate pre-pass or inside the main
  loop.
- Whether to add an "after" live test to `tests/live.rs` (ignored by default) or keep the probe only.

## GATE 1: spec approval

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-20-sma-820-gemini-merge-same-role-contents-design.md` (in the `sma-820` worktree, not committed yet).

**Challenger verdict:** APPROVE WITH CHANGES. It found 1 BLOCKER, 5 MAJOR, 8 MINOR and 5 questions.

### Two decisions for you
Both change what you approved before.

1. **The pairing rule: FIFO, not LIFO.** The ticket says "the most recent earlier call that has no result yet". Take two calls in one round that share `fc_0`, first `search`, then `pay`. With LIFO, both names are wrong. `main` gets one of the two correct. Core pairs by the **earliest** open call. I checked this rule in `resume_exec.rs:200-220` and `deferral.rs:585-620`. **I recommend FIFO.** It also fixes the cross-turn case in the ticket.
2. **A second result for one call is now dropped, with a warning.** Before, it took the name of the most recent earlier call. Core's `agent_view` also drops such a result. This rule also prevents a merged content with more responses than calls.

### Findings added to the spec
- **BLOCKER, live check.** The spec now gives 14 exact probe shapes and a pass rule (HTTP 200, `STOP`, and an answer that uses the tool result). The probe runs **before** the code. If Gemini rejects the merged shapes 3 or 6, I stop and come back to you. I added shapes 10–14 to `probe.sh`.
- **The "after" check.** An ignored live test in `tests/live.rs` is now mandatory. It sends the requests through the real translator.
- **The test plan.** I added same-round `fc_0`, `ToolUse` parts, out-of-order results, the duplicate result, a result before its call, nested results mixed with text, `System` between user messages, and empty `Text`.
- **One pass is now required.** A pre-pass keyed by call id would bring the bug back.
- **The scope includes `mod.rs`,** because of its inline asserts on `contents[3]` and `[4]`.
- **Empty `Text` parts are dropped.** SMA-804 §5.3 asks for this, and the merge would otherwise put `{"text":""}` next to a `functionResponse`.
- **A result before its call has its own error message.** The commit message names it.
- **Known limits are written down.** These are open deferred calls in a `CompactingSession` summary (probe shape 14), and `ParallelAgent` replays with sibling `fc_0` ids. This spec does not fix either one.
- **The Intent lists all the sources of adjacency.** The spec also states the reason for the `stream.rs` non-goal, and that no docs, book or README edit is needed.

### Not added
- Joining adjacent user texts with `\n`. I keep separate parts, and the probe shows whether Gemini accepts them.
- Gemini 3 and Vertex in the probe. Gemini 3 needs thought signatures, which is a separate problem (D3). Vertex uses the same translator.

### Still open
The probe has not run. The auto-mode classifier denied my read of `.env`. Please run:

```
! (set -a; . /Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.env; set +a; bash /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-smaschek-dev-paigasus-paigasus-helikon/a905e743-8ae6-4dc6-b611-23137fb84e38/scratchpad/sma820/probe.sh gemini-2.5-flash)
```

Please approve the spec and choose FIFO or LIFO. You can also ask for more changes, or run the challenge again with `/challenge-spec`. I start the plan only after your approval **and** the probe output.

input.new_string:
### Results before the fix (2026-11-20, Developer API, hand-made bodies)

`gemini-2.5-flash` and `gemini-2.5-flash-lite`: HTTP 404 on every shape, "no longer available to
new users". The probe therefore ran on `gemini-3.8-flash`.

`gemini-3.8-flash` with no `thoughtSignature`: HTTP 400 "Function call is missing a
thought_signature in functionCall parts" on every shape in which the call is in the current turn
(1, 3, 5-14). Shapes 2 and 4 returned HTTP 200 / `STOP`, because the trailing user text moves the
call into an earlier turn, and Gemini checks signatures only in the current turn.

`gemini-3.8-flash` with the documented dummy signature `skip_thought_signature_validator` on each
`functionCall` part:

| Shape | Result |
|---|---|
| 1 baseline | 200 STOP, uses the result |
| 2 SMA-804 today (two adjacent `user`) | 200 STOP, uses the result |
| 3 SMA-804 merged | 200 STOP, uses the result |
| 4 three adjacent `user` | 200 STOP |
| 5 parallel today | 200 STOP |
| 6 parallel merged | 200 STOP |
| 7 response name differs from call name | **400 "Request contains an invalid argument."** |
| 8 repeated `fc_0`, correct names | 200 STOP |
| 9 repeated `fc_0`, today's wrong name | **400 "Request contains an invalid argument."** |
| 10 `model[text, fc]` | 200 STOP |
| 11 merged, responses reordered | 200 STOP |
| 12 `user[fr, {"text": ""}]` | 200 STOP |
| 13 two responses for one call | 200 STOP |
| 14 merged, one call with no response | 200 STOP, the model calls `search` again |

What this means:

- Defect 1 (adjacent same-role contents) causes no failure on `gemini-3.8-flash`. Both the split and
  the merged shapes are accepted. The merge stays as the ticket requires: it is safe on the API, it
  gives the shape that Gemini itself sends, and no official source promises that the split shape
  stays accepted.
- Defect 2 (wrong name) is a **hard failure**: HTTP 400 on the next model call. Part 2 is the fix
  that matters for users.
- Gemini accepts a second response for one call (13). The translator still drops it, to match core.
- Shape 14 (an open call with no response) is accepted. Known limit 1 causes no API error.

### Out of scope, found by the probe

The Gemini provider does not read or send `thoughtSignature` (no match in `crates/`). With a
current Gemini model, every request in which the current turn holds a `functionCall` gets HTTP 400.
So tool loops on Gemini 3.x fail at the second model call. The model ids in the crate docs and in
`tests/live.rs` (`gemini-2.5-flash`) are not available to new users. A separate Linear issue tracks
both.

### After the fix

The live test in `tests/live.rs` runs through the real translator. Because the translator sends no
thought signatures, each history in the test ends with a user text after the last tool result, so
no call is in the current turn. Shape 9 shows that Gemini checks names in earlier turns too, so the
cross-turn `fc_0` history still tests the name fix. The test model defaults to `gemini-3.8-flash`
(override with `GEMINI_MODEL_ID`); the default of the existing `dev_model()` changes from
`gemini-2.5-flash` to `gemini-3.8-flash`, because the old default returns 404 for new users.

- After: _pending (runs at the end of implementation)._

Scope of the check: Developer API only. Vertex uses the same translator.

You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow.
